blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a novel and dangerous attack on the Control Area Network (CAN) protocol used in modern vehicles, called the 'bus-off attack'. Unlike prior attacks, this method doesn't require reverse engineering vehicle-specific CAN messages, works universally across all vehicles, and bypasses MAC-based protections and state-of-the-art intrusion detection systems (IDS). The attack exploits CAN's built-in error-handling mechanisms, particularly the transmit error counter (TEC), to force a targeted ECU into a 'bus-off' state where it is permanently disabled. The author emphasizes the attack's ease of deployment, its potential safety implications for drivers, and the urgency to develop countermeasures, noting that even future security-enhanced in-vehicle networks may remain vulnerable. The paper argues for concerted efforts from academia and industry to address this flaw.
paper_title: Stealing Cars: Secure CAN Message Specification using CAN Message Reverse Engineering
paper_abstract: 1 Modern Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) are equipped with an increasing number of Electronic Control Units (ECUs), many of which produce large amounts of data. Data is exchanged between ECUs via an in-vehicle network, with the Controller Area Network (CAN) bus being the de facto standard in contemporary vehicles. Furthermore, CAVs have not only physical interfaces but also increased data connectivity to the Internet via their Telematic Control Units (TCUs), enabling remote access via mobile devices. It is also possible to tap into, and read/write data from/to the CAN bus, as data transmitted on the CAN bus is not encrypted. This naturally generates concerns about automotive cybersecurity. One commonality among most vehicular security attacks reported to date is that they ultimately require write access to the CAN bus. In order to cause targeted and intentional changes in vehicle behavior, malicious CAN injection attacks require knowledge of the CAN message format. However, since this format is proprietary to OEMs and can differ even among different models of a single make of vehicle, one must manually reverse-engineer the CAN message format of each vehicle they target — a time-consuming and tedious process that does not scale. To mitigate this difficulty, we develop LibreCAN, which can translate most CAN messages with minimal effort. Our extensive evaluation on multiple vehicles demonstrates LibreCAN’s efficiency in terms of accuracy, coverage, required manual effort and scalability to any vehicle. Nearly all functions inside a modern vehicle, even in more traditionally mechanical domains like the powertrain, are controlled electronically. Moreover, purely electronic systems have become more prevalent as the number of sensors present in a vehicle has increased, particularly given the rise of Advanced Driver Assistance (ADAS) systems.
